title: Why Russell Westbrook is a better passer than Steph Curry
text:
NBA fans argue about everything, who’s the GOAT, who’s more clutch, who locks up on defense. But today, we’re looking at a different debate: who’s the better passer, Russell Westbrook or Stephen Curry? At first glance, it seems easy. Russ has the triple-doubles and crazy assist numbers. Steph is known for deep threes and off-ball movement. But raw assist stats don’t tell the whole story. To really figure it out, we’ll look at assists per game, assist-to-turnover ratio, and how scoring and passing go together. So let’s break it down. Russ vs. Steph: who’s the better passer?


Code
library(tidyverse)
library(hoopR)
library(ggrepel)
library(ggtext)

Players<- load_nba_player_box(2009:2024) |> filter(team_name!="All-Stars") |> 
filter(team_name !="Team LeBron") |> 
filter(team_name!="Team Giannis") |> 
filter(team_name!="Leb") |> 
filter(team_name!="Team Stephen")

Players <- Players |> 
  mutate(free_throw_assists = sample(0:5, n(), replace = TRUE))
seasontotals <- Players |> 
  group_by(athlete_display_name,season,team_name) |> 
  summarise(
    totalminutes=sum(minutes, na.rm=TRUE),
    totalpoints=sum(points, na.rm=TRUE),
    totalassists=sum(assists, na.rm =TRUE),
    totalturnovers=sum(turnovers, na.rm =TRUE),
    games_played = n(), 
    assist_per_game=sum(assists, na.rm = TRUE) / n()
  ) |>
  mutate(assist_to_turnover=totalassists/totalturnovers)
RW<-seasontotals |> filter(athlete_display_name=="Russell Westbrook")
SC<-seasontotals |> filter(athlete_display_name=="Stephen Curry")

ggplot() + 
  geom_line(
    data=RW,
    aes(x=season,y=assist_to_turnover),
    color="#007AC1"
    )+
    geom_line(
    data=SC,
    aes(x=season,y=assist_to_turnover),
    color="#FFC72C"
    )+


  labs(
    title = "Russ at his best is better than Curry, but at his worst...",
    x = "",
    y = "Assist-to-Turnover Ratio",
    color = "Player",
    subtitle="When looking at these two point guards Curry is as steady can be, while peak Russ is better bad Russ is way worse.", 
    caption="Source: HoopR | By: A.J. Morgan"
    ) +
  theme_minimal() + 
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold"),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 7), 
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size=9), 
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    plot.title.position = "plot"
    ) 









As you see from this chart when looking at Westbrook and Curry their styles couldn’t be more different. Westbrook is a high-energy, high-risk playmaker who thrives in transition and racks up assists,but also turns the ball over a lot. Curry is more controlled, using his gravity and smart reads to make safer, efficient passes, even if he doesn’t get as many assists. Assist-to-turnover ratio is a great stat to look at, however it doesn’t show the full picture. To really see how they’ve impacted the game as passers, we need to look at their assists over time. Who stayed consistent? Who peaked when it mattered? Let’s check out this step chart to find out.


Code
logs <- read_csv("https://hoopr.sportsdataverse.org/")
careerassists<-Players |> 
  group_by(athlete_display_name,season) |> 
  summarise(total_assists=sum(assists, na.rm=TRUE)) |> 
  ungroup() |> 
  group_by(athlete_display_name) |> 
  arrange(season) |> 
  mutate(Cumassists = cumsum(total_assists))
RWassists<-careerassists|> filter(athlete_display_name=="Russell Westbrook")
SCassists<-careerassists|> filter(athlete_display_name=="Stephen Curry")
ggplot() + 
  geom_step(data=careerassists, aes(x=season, y=Cumassists, group=athlete_display_name), color="lightgrey") +
  geom_step(data=RWassists, aes(x=season, y=Cumassists, group=athlete_display_name), color="#007AC1") +
  geom_step(data=SCassists, aes(x=season, y=Cumassists, group=athlete_display_name), color="#FFC72C") +
  geom_point(data=RWassists |> filter(season == max(season)), aes(x=season, y=Cumassists, group=athlete_display_name), color="#007AC1") +
  geom_point(data=SCassists|> filter(season == max(season)), aes(x=season, y=Cumassists, group=athlete_display_name), color="#FFC72C") +
  geom_text_repel(data=RWassists |> filter(season == max(season)), aes(x=season, y=Cumassists, group=athlete_display_name, label = athlete_display_name)) +
  geom_text_repel(data=SCassists|> filter(season == max(season)), aes(x=season, y=Cumassists, group=athlete_display_name, label = athlete_display_name))+ 
  labs(
    title = "Russ and Curry assists overtime shows Westbrooks consistancy",
    x = "Years",
    y = "Assist overtime",
    color = "Player",
    subtitle="Through the first half of their careers they're pretty close however after 2020 westbrook really seperates himself.", 
    caption="Source: HoopR | By: A.J. Morgan"
    ) +
  theme_minimal() + 
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 13, face = "bold"),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 7), 
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size=9), 
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    plot.title.position = "plot"
    )









Westbrook has the most total assists over time against some of the toughest defenses in the league. While Curry’s assist numbers are solid and consistent, Russ’s volume and pace put him well ahead of not just Steph, but most guards across the NBA. However raw assist totals only show one side of the story. What happens when you factor in scoring too? This final chart looks at both total points and total assists, giving us a fuller picture of overall offensive impact.


Code
ggplot() + 
  geom_point(data=seasontotals, aes(x=totalpoints, y=totalassists), color="lightgrey")+
  geom_point(data=RW, aes(x=totalpoints, y=totalassists), color="#007AC1")+
  geom_point(data=SC, aes(x=totalpoints, y=totalassists), color="#FFC72C")+ 
  labs(
    title = "Russ vs Curry Scoring and Passing",
    x = "Total Points",
    y = "Total Assists",
    color = "Player",
    subtitle = "When looking at scoring and passing <span style = 'color:#007AC1;'>Russell</span> stays ahead of<span style = 'color:#FFC72C;'> Curry</span> when it comes to scoring and passing.", 
    caption="Source: HoopR | By: A.J. Morgan"
    ) +
  theme_minimal() + 
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 20, face = "bold"),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 8), 
    plot.subtitle = element_textbox_simple(size=10), 
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    plot.title.position = "plot"
    )









And once again, Westbrook stands out, not just as a passer, but as a dual threat who racks up numbers in both areas at a level few others can match. So, who’s the better passer? The numbers don’t lie. Curry might be the more efficient playmaker, however Westbrook’s total impact as a passer ,from volume, to consistency, to how he pairs it with his scoring, gives him the edge. After this Where does Curry stand? Still one of the smartest and most creative guards in the league, but in this debate, the edge goes to Russell Westbrook.

title: WHich team has the best chance for this years Playoffs
text:
The NBA Playoffs are finally here, and it’s time to figure out who’s actually built to make a deep run. NBA fans love making predictions, who’s gonna sweep, who’s getting bounced early, and who’s making it to the Finals. But instead of guessing, let’s actually look at the numbers. The playoffs are all about pressure, and not every team is built to handle it. Some squads feed off the energy of a packed arena. Others find another gear when they’re at home in the postseason. Let’s break it down.


Code
library(tidyverse)
library(hoopR)
library(ggrepel)
library(ggtext)
library(ggalt)
library(janitor)

team <- load_nba_team_box(2015:2025)

schedule <- load_nba_schedule(2015:2025)

advstats <- read_csv("advstats2025.csv") |> 
  clean_names() |> 
  remove_empty(which = c("cols", "rows")) |> 
  filter(team != "League Average") |> 
  mutate(team=gsub("*","",team,fixed = TRUE))

regularseasonwins <- schedule |> 
  filter(season_type == 2) |> 
  filter(home_display_name != "TBD") |> 
  group_by(home_display_name) |> 
  summarize(
    home_games = n(),
    home_wins = length(home_winner[home_winner==TRUE])
  ) |> 
  mutate(
    home_win_pct = (home_wins/home_games)
  ) |> 
  arrange(desc(home_win_pct))

postseasonwins <- schedule |> 
  filter(season_type == 3) |> 
  filter(home_display_name != "TBD") |> 
  group_by(home_display_name) |> 
  summarize(
    postseason_home_games = n(),
    postseason_home_wins = length(home_winner[home_winner==TRUE])
  ) |> 
  mutate(
    postseason_home_win_pct = (postseason_home_wins/postseason_home_games)
  ) |> 
  arrange(desc(postseason_home_win_pct))

advantage <- postseasonwins |> inner_join(regularseasonwins)

attendance <- schedule |> 
  filter(season_type == 3) |> 
  filter(season != 2020) |> 
  group_by(home_short_display_name) |> 
  summarize(
    avg_attendance = mean(attendance, na.rm=TRUE)
  ) |> 
  arrange(desc(avg_attendance)) |> 
  filter(home_short_display_name != "TBD")

bars <- attendance |> filter(home_short_display_name == "Thunder" | home_short_display_name == "Cavaliers" | home_short_display_name == "Celtics")

ggplot() + 
  geom_bar(data=attendance, aes(x=reorder(home_short_display_name, avg_attendance), weight=avg_attendance), fill="#D3D3D3") +
  geom_bar(data=bars, aes(x=reorder(home_short_display_name, avg_attendance), weight=avg_attendance), fill="#8B0000") +  
  coord_flip() + 
  labs(
    title = "What teams have the best average attendance",
    x = "",
    y = "Attendance numbers",
    subtitle = "From Chicago to Philly, these teams bring in the biggest crowds night after night, win or lose.", 
    caption="Source: HoopR | By: A.J. Morgan"
    ) +
  theme_minimal() + 
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 18, face = "bold"),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 8), 
    plot.subtitle = element_textbox_simple(size=10), 
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    plot.title.position = "plot"
    )









Looking at this chart, it’s clear which teams bring in the biggest crowds. The Bulls, Pistons, and Mavs are at the top, and having that kind of fan support night after night definitely matters, especially in the playoffs. A packed arena brings energy, momentum, and can rattle the other team when things get intense. That said, just because you’ve got a sold-out crowd doesn’t mean you’re winning games. Attendance shows who’s got a strong home environment, but it doesn’t tell us if teams actually take advantage of it. To figure that out, we need to see who steps up at home when the lights are brightest. Next let’s check out playoff home win percentage.


Code
ggplot() + 
  geom_dumbbell(
    data=advantage, 
    aes(y=reorder(home_display_name,postseason_home_win_pct), x=home_win_pct, xend=postseason_home_win_pct),
     size = 2,
    colour = "grey",
    colour_x = "#1D428A",
    colour_xend = "#C8102E") +
  labs(
    title = "What teams have a better home win percentage in the playoffs, compared to the regular season",
    x = "Regular Season vs Playoff Home win Percentage",
    y = "",
    color = "Player",
    subtitle = " Some teams turn it up when it matters most, others fall off. This chart shows who steps up at home once the postseason hits.", 
    caption="Source: HoopR | By: A.J. Morgan"
    ) +
  theme_minimal() + 
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 9.2, face = "bold"),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 8), 
    plot.subtitle = element_textbox_simple(size=7), 
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    plot.title.position = "plot"
    )









Now this chart shows who actually shows up at home when the pressure’s on. The red dots are each team’s playoff home win percentage, and the blue ones are their regular season home win percentage. If the red dot is higher, it means that team plays better at home in the playoffs than they do during the regular season. Teams like the Warriors, Cavs, and Thunder really stand out, they know how to lock in when it counts. Playing at home in the postseason isn’t just about having a crowd, it’s about taking advantage of it. Not every team does. Look toward the bottom, teams like the Pistons, Bulls, and Pelicans either stay the same or actually get worse at home in the playoffs. This is the kind of stat that matters in a seven-game series. If a team consistently takes care of business at home when it matters most, that gives them a serious shot at going deep.


Code
adv_labels <- advstats |> 
  filter(team=="Boston Celtics" | team=="Cleveland Cavaliers" | team=="Oklahoma City Thunder")

bc <-  advstats |> 
  filter(team=="Boston Celtics")

cc <-  advstats |> 
  filter(team=="Cleveland Cavaliers")

okc <-  advstats |> 
  filter(team=="Oklahoma City Thunder")

ggplot() + 
  geom_point(
    data=advstats, 
    aes(x=o_rtg, y=d_rtg, size=w), 
    alpha = .3,
    color = "grey"
    ) +
  geom_point(
    data=bc, 
    aes(x=o_rtg, y=d_rtg, size=w), 
    alpha = .3,
    color="#007A33"
    ) +
  geom_point(
    data=cc, 
    aes(x=o_rtg, y=d_rtg, size=w), 
    alpha = .3,
    color="#860038"
    ) +
  geom_point(
    data=okc, 
    aes(x=o_rtg, y=d_rtg, size=w), 
    alpha = .3,
    color="#007AC1"
    ) +
  geom_vline(xintercept =114.5) + 
  geom_hline(yintercept = 114.5)+
  geom_text_repel(data=adv_labels, 
    aes(x=o_rtg, y=d_rtg, label=team)
    )+ 
  labs(
    x="Offensive Rating", 
    y="Defensive Rating", 
    title="These Teams Are Built for a Finals Run", 
    subtitle="Cleveland, Boston, and OKC don’t just score, they lock up on defense too. That balance is what makes them real contenders.", 
    caption="Source: HoopR | A.J. Morgan"
    ) +
  theme_minimal() + 
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 21, face = "bold"),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 8), 
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size=7.5), 
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    plot.title.position = "plot"
    ) 









This chart goes beyond just win totals, it shows how efficient teams are on offense and defense. The teams you want to focus on are in the bottom right corner, where high offensive rating meets strong defense. Boston, Cleveland, and OKC all land there, showing they’re not just talented, but super balanced. That kind of two-way play is what matters in a seven-game series. Sure, other teams might have loud fan bases or crazy offenses, but that doesn’t always translate to postseason success. If you’re trying to figure out who’s really built for a deep playoff run, these three teams are the safest bets.
